\begin{abstract}
Recursive LLM generation shifts \emph{where} text sits in distributional space but leaves \emph{how} it is shaped nearly unchanged, and this asymmetry is consistent across five model families spanning 0.6B to 8B parameters.
We term this \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): under standard decoding, mean entropy and lexical diversity drift monotonically with generation depth while entropy max and vocabulary tail slope show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
Prior work on iterative generation tracks aggregate convergence without separating what changes from what is preserved; DDR provides this decomposition and enables coarse depth classification (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+): a 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 (95\% CI [.688, .700]) under leave-one-generator-out evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, at lower cost than multi-detector alternatives.
Despite measurable distributional drift, equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) confirms no downstream training quality degradation.
The depth signal degrades under instruction tuning; current applicability is restricted to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When the output of a language model is fed back as input to another (or the same) model, the resulting generation chain defines a discrete dynamical system over text distributions.
How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
Understanding this evolution is fundamental to characterizing how language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with implications for model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} and data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} as model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} (an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}).
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, but none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components; our work addresses this gap in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.

Because drifting features capture the progressive location shift while stationary features provide a stable reference, combining them yields a classifier that generalizes across generators: binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp and a 4-detector ensemble at 2.4$\times$ lower computational cost.

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary detection to ordinal depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We decompose inference-chain drift into structurally distinct components: central-tendency features drift monotonically ($d = 0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable ($d < 0.10$), a decomposition absent from existing attractor dynamics and model collapse analyses. A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this \emph{differential depth response} achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains.
    \item Comprehensive evaluation reveals that DDR is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), is prompt-type modulated (continuation $>$ elaboration), and is absent in instruction-tuned models; equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) confirms no downstream quality degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), but QLoRA on instruct data (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91 vs.\ XGBoost 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal; alignment compresses the handcrafted feature margins DDR exploits while richer representations partially recover.

\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

Do existing detection methods already capture depth signal?
To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Feat.} & \textbf{3-cl F1} & \textbf{Bin F1} & \textbf{ms/text} \\
\midrule
4-det.\ + surface     & 6 & \textbf{0.795} & \textbf{0.708} & 22.8 \\
4-detector ens.\      & 4 & 0.785 & 0.700 & 22.8 \\
7-feature (ours)      & 7 & 0.774 & 0.705 & \textbf{9.7} \\
Avg-LogProb           & 1 & 0.707 & 0.673 & N/A \\
FastDetectGPT         & 1 & 0.660 & 0.569 & N/A \\
LD-Score              & 1 & 0.630 & 0.675 & N/A \\
Binoculars            & 1 & 0.411 & 0.539 & N/A \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Depth classification (8-gen LOGO, pooled evaluation; slightly higher than per-generator macro average in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Identical XGBoost configuration. 7-feature: one 410M model (905\,MB); 4-det ensembles: two models, 1.4B params (2{,}868\,MB). Individual detection scores (N/A) share the reference-model forward pass; per-method timing is not separately profiled.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble exceeds all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp).
Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher binary F1 (0.708 vs.\ 0.705) at 2.4$\times$ inference cost, suggesting depth information is implicitly encoded in distributional divergence measures.
DDR's contribution is not classification performance but decomposing depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   I am the independent Research Reviewer (审查员) for the gen-depth-fingerprint project targeting EMNLP 2026 ARR submission (DDL: 2026-05-25). All output must be in Chinese. My role is to independently verify experiment conclusions, audit paper claims against raw data, check GPU compliance, and report findings to the Director via `reviewer_post_to_director`. In this session I was tasked with:
   - Verifying the page limit fix (Conclusion overflow to p9 — previously CRITICAL)
   - Executing final PDF visual check across all main-text and appendix pages
   - Evaluating 4 GPU experiment directions for idle 4× RTX 5090
   - Deep evaluation of narrative/contribution framing for 3.0→3.5 score improvement
   - Full coherence review after Paper Agent applied 3 narrative optimization levers
   - Clean read verification after Director fixed 7 issues I identified
   - Monitoring compilation/sync workers
   - Auditing experiment utilization (42 successful experiments vs paper citations)

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **DDR (Differential Depth Response)**: Tri-partition of 7 features into drifting (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax; |ρ|>0.60, d=0.76–1.17), intermediate (entropy_std; d=0.55), near-stationary (entropy_max, tail_decay, entropy_min; d<0.10)
   - **LOGO**: Leave-One-Generator-Out cross-validation. Primary metric: binary F1=0.694 (gen-1 vs gen-2+), 8 generators from 5 families
   - **EMNLP 2026 ARR**: Strict 8-page main text limit, unlimited references, Limitations/Ethics exempt
   - **Location-shape decoupling**: Core insight — recursive generation shifts NLL distribution location while preserving shape
   - **Concurrent work differentiation**: 3 ACL 2025 papers (Broken Telephone, Markovian Chains, Attractor Cycles) characterize THAT convergence occurs; this paper characterizes WHAT converges vs what is preserved
   - **QLoRA**: End-to-end depth classifier. 3-class F1=0.905 on 6-gen LOGO; instruct recovery 0.888–0.907
   - **TOST equivalence testing**: Downstream curation ≡ random subsampling (±2%, p<0.001)
   - **Primary metric discipline**: Results L9 designates leak-free binary F1=0.694 as primary; 0.764 cross-model is secondary (5-gen subset, sample-level CV, has caveats)

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **artifacts/_project/paper/abstract.tex** (final version, 15:58 UTC)
     - Surprise-first opening: "Recursive LLM generation shifts *where* text sits in distributional space but leaves *how* it is shaped nearly unchanged"
     - F1=0.694 leads (primary metric), 0.764 secondary
     - TOST downstream result included
     - Base-only scope limitation restored at L7
     - Issue: "vocabulary tail slope" terminology inconsistent with "tail decay" used elsewhere (W-new-1)
   
   - **artifacts/_project/paper/introduction.tex** (final version, 15:58 UTC)
     - L10: Concurrent work gap — "none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components"
     - L14: Mechanistic hypothesis — "one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape"
     - L16: "outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3pp and a 4-detector ensemble at 2.4× lower computational cost" — Issue: implies outperforming 4-detector ensemble but 7-feature actually loses (0.705 vs 0.708) (W-new-2)
     - L22: Temperature claim fixed — "robust within t∈[0.5,0.7] but degrades at t=0.9 (−9.3 to −26.0pp)"
     - L22: Reference fixed — `Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}` instead of broken `\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}`
   
   - **artifacts/_project/paper/discussion.tex** (final version, 15:58 UTC)
     - L4: Mechanistic intuition — "mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs" (direction corrected from "mean log-probability decreases")
     - L15: QLoRA instruct recovery restored — "QLoRA on instruct data (F1=0.89-0.91 vs XGBoost 0.58-0.73) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal"
   
   - **artifacts/_project/paper/conclusion.tex** (final version, 15:58 UTC)
     - L5: Primary metric leads — "leak-free binary F1=0.694 under LOGO evaluation, 0.764 on cross-model chains"
     - L6: Forward-looking — "depth signal may arise in any iterative autoregressive process with fixed decoding, a hypothesis testable beyond text generation"

     - L9: "We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs gen-2+)=0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout"

     - L31: "our tri-partition reveals what converges (location) versus what remains stable (shape)"

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow$ mismatch: F1 from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013\,pp; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though richer representations recover substantially more signal (QLoRA F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}).
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base), but QLoRA on instruct data (F1\,=\,0.89--0.91 vs.\ XGBoost 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}) indicates instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the signal; alignment compresses the handcrafted feature margins DDR exploits while richer representations partially recover.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When the output of a language model is fed back as input to another (or the same) model, the resulting generation chain defines a discrete dynamical system over text distributions.
How do the distributional properties of generated text evolve across successive steps of this recursion?
Understanding this evolution is fundamental to characterizing how language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with implications for model collapse theory \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} and data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} as model outputs increasingly re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} (an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}).
Yet existing detection methods \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide only binary real-vs-synthetic decisions, conflating qualitatively different material: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by coarse ordinal depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
Concurrent studies characterize convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}, but none decompose the drift into structurally distinct components; our work addresses this gap in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven shaping) that obscure the distributional dynamics of recursive generation; preliminary experiments confirm substantially degraded depth signal under instruction tuning (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, central-tendency and diversity features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay) show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation producing a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution; one hypothesis is that the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constrain distributional shape under standard decoding regimes, while each successive generation compresses the location toward the model's preferred output distribution.

Because drifting features capture the progressive location shift while stationary features provide a stable reference, combining them yields a classifier that generalizes across generators: binary F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and 0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp and a 4-detector ensemble at 2.4$\times$ lower computational cost.

Our contributions are threefold:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary detection to ordinal depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+), and construct an evaluation suite of 37K texts from eight generators spanning five model families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We decompose inference-chain drift into structurally distinct components: central-tendency features drift monotonically ($d = 0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features remain an order of magnitude more stable ($d < 0.10$), a decomposition absent from existing attractor dynamics and model collapse analyses. A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this \emph{differential depth response} achieves binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains.
    \item Comprehensive evaluation reveals that DDR is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp), is prompt-type modulated (continuation $>$ elaboration), and is absent in instruction-tuned models; equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) confirms no downstream quality degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
\end{enumerate}

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Recursive LLM generation shifts \emph{where} text sits in distributional space but leaves \emph{how} it is shaped nearly unchanged, and this asymmetry is consistent across five model families spanning 0.6B to 8B parameters.
We term this \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): under standard decoding, mean entropy and lexical diversity drift monotonically with generation depth while entropy max and vocabulary tail slope show an order-of-magnitude smaller effect size.
Prior work on iterative generation tracks aggregate convergence without separating what changes from what is preserved; DDR provides this decomposition and enables coarse depth classification (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+): a 7-feature ensemble achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 (95\% CI [.688, .700]) under leave-one-generator-out evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, at lower cost than multi-detector alternatives.
Despite measurable distributional drift, equivalence testing (TOST $\pm$2\%, $p < 0.001$) confirms no downstream training quality degradation.
The depth signal degrades under instruction tuning; current applicability is restricted to base models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Independent-Seed Control}
\label{app:seed-control}

To test for topic-level leakage from shared seeds across generators, we construct an independent-seed evaluation where Pythia-2.8B and OLMo-2-1B use completely disjoint Wikipedia seed pools (500 seeds each, zero overlap).
Each generator produces depth-0 through depth-4 chains on its own seed pool; features are extracted with the same Pythia-410M reference model.
We then train a 7-feature XGBoost classifier on one generator's data and test on the other, in both directions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Setting} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule
Pythia-2.8B $\rightarrow$ OLMo-2-1B & 0.695 & [0.673, 0.717] \\
OLMo-2-1B $\rightarrow$ Pythia-2.8B & 0.666 & [0.643, 0.689] \\
\midrule
Independent-seed average & 0.680 & --- \\
Shared-seed LOGO (reference) & 0.694 & [0.688, 0.700] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Independent-seed cross-generator evaluation (binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Disjoint seed pools eliminate any possibility of topic-based leakage. The average independent-seed F1 (0.680) is within 1.4\,pp of the shared-seed LOGO baseline (0.694). The classifier thus captures generative degradation patterns rather than seed-specific topic content.}
\label{tab:seed-control}
\end{table}

The small gap ($-$1.4\,pp) between independent-seed and shared-seed evaluation falls within bootstrap confidence intervals, and both directions individually exceed 0.66.
Combined with the seed-level demeaning control (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), these results provide converging evidence that depth classification is driven by distributional properties of recursive generation, not topic identity.

Now I have a clear picture. The appendix_seed_control.tex argues "not topic identity" based on independent seed pools (plan-051) and seed demeaning. But the review-exp-b-topic-drift experiment has DIRECT evidence: it computed semantic similarity (cosine of embeddings) between generations at different depths and showed that semantic similarity is high (increases with depth, 0.622→0.859) while distributional features still discriminate.

This is a much stronger argument than the indirect "disjoint seeds" argument. The semantic similarity data directly tests "is depth signal = topic shift?" and the answer is clear: the text becomes MORE semantically similar at deeper depths, yet distributional features still separate them.

\subsection*{Instruction-Tuned Model Results}

Table~\ref{tab:instruct} summarizes depth classification under instruction tuning for three model families.
All results use within-model 5-fold CV on single-generator chains; LOGO evaluation is available for two models but uses earlier generator subsets (5--6 generators), so cross-model numbers are not directly comparable across rows.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Depth classification: base vs.\ instruction-tuned models (within-model 5-fold CV). $\rho$: Spearman correlation of entropy mean with depth. Rev.: number of features (out of 7) whose $\rho$ reverses sign under instruction tuning.}
\label{tab:instruct}
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcc cc cc c}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{3-class F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Binary F1}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\boldsymbol{\rho}$\textbf{(ent.\ mean)}} & \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \cmidrule(lr){4-5} \cmidrule(lr){6-7}
\textbf{Model} & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & Base & Instruct & \textbf{Rev.} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B       & 0.754 & 0.575 & 0.845 & 0.813 & $-$0.64 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & 0.769 & 0.732 & 0.861 & 0.875 & $-$0.60 & $+$0.48 & 6/7 \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & 0.742 & 0.544 & 0.849 & 0.838 & $-$0.63 & $+$0.23 & 3/7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Instruction tuning degrades 3-class F1 by 3.7--19.9\,pp across all three families, while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) changes remain small ($|\Delta| \leq 3.2$\,pp).
The asymmetry indicates that instruction tuning primarily disrupts the gen-0/gen-1 boundary (human vs.\ first-generation), consistent with RLHF shifting the output distribution away from human-like text.
Entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign for all three models ($-0.60$--$-0.64$ base $\rightarrow$ $+0.23$--$+0.48$ instruct), and 6 of 7 features reverse for OLMo and Qwen vs.\ 3 of 7 for Llama.
This pattern is consistent with instruction tuning shifting the generation attractor rather than eliminating iterative dynamics (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Retraining on instruction-tuned data.}
To test whether the depth signal persists under instruction tuning with reversed polarity, we retrain the XGBoost classifier on instruction-tuned feature data (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-retrain}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Classification recovery under instruction-tuned retraining (binary-only: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, gen-0 excluded from training and evaluation). Base$\rightarrow$Inst: base-trained classifier tested on instruct data. Note: Table~\ref{tab:instruct} reports higher instruct binary F1 (e.g., OLMo 0.813) because it uses 3-class training with binary evaluation, where gen-0 in training helps the classifier learn the feature space.}
\label{tab:instruct-retrain}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Base$\rightarrow$Inst} & \textbf{Retrained} & \textbf{$\Delta$} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B-Inst   & 0.321 & 0.590 & $+$0.269 \\
Qwen3-1.7B-Inst  & 0.500 & 0.660 & $+$0.160 \\
Qwen3-0.6B-Inst  & 0.532 & 0.600 & $+$0.068 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Retraining recovers substantial within-model performance ($+$6.8--26.9\,pp), but the retrained F1 (0.590--0.660) remains below base-model levels (0.69--0.72).
Three-generator instruct LOGO yields binary F1\,=\,0.487, indicating weak cross-generator transfer under instruction tuning.

\paragraph{DDR structure under instruction tuning.}
$k{=}2$ clustering in $(|\rho|, d)$ space on pooled instruct features yields silhouette\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.632 for base models), indicating that the clean drifting/non-drifting partition is substantially compressed.
The compression is model-dependent: OLMo-Instruct shows near-zero $|\rho|$ for TTR and hapax (0.006, 0.025), while Qwen instruct models retain moderate correlations ($|\rho|{=}0.48$--$0.53$).
Cross-condition transfer is near chance in both directions (base$\rightarrow$instruct binary F1\,=\,0.490; instruct$\rightarrow$base F1\,=\,0.454), with the asymmetry ($-$0.036) suggesting that instruct-trained features generalize even less to base distributions than the reverse.
These results indicate that instruction tuning compresses the feature-space structure underlying DDR rather than simply reversing feature directions.

\paragraph{End-to-end instruct classification.}
To test whether depth signal persists at the token level despite summary-statistic degradation, we apply the QLoRA end-to-end classifier (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) to instruction-tuned data using within-model 5-fold stratified CV (Table~\ref{tab:instruct-qlora}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{End-to-end QLoRA vs.\ XGBoost on instruction-tuned data (within-model 5-fold CV, Qwen3-0.6B backbone). Base QLoRA rows shown for reference only; instruct sets ($N{\approx}4.4$--$5.0$K) are approximately twice the base sets ($N{\approx}2.3$K), so cross-condition comparison is confounded by training set size.}
\label{tab:instruct-qlora}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{3-class F1}} & & \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-3}
\textbf{Model} & XGB & QLoRA & $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ & \textbf{$N$} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B-Inst   & 0.575 & 0.888\,$\pm$\,0.007 & $+$31.3\,pp & 4{,}429 \\
Qwen3-1.7B-Inst  & 0.732 & 0.907\,$\pm$\,0.008 & $+$17.5\,pp & 4{,}963 \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B (base) &       & 0.859\,$\pm$\,0.004 &             & 2{,}379 \\
Qwen3-1.7B (base)&       & 0.904\,$\pm$\,0.009 &             & 2{,}291 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The XGBoost-to-QLoRA gap on the same instruct data is substantial ($+$17.5 to $+$31.3\,pp), indicating that depth signal persists at the token level under instruction tuning but is inaccessible to the seven summary statistics; the degradation reported in Table~\ref{tab:instruct} reflects a feature-level limitation rather than signal absence.

1	To assess whether depth signal extends beyond handcrafted features, we fine-tune a pretrained language model end-to-end as a depth classifier using QLoRA \cite{qlora}.
2	
3	\paragraph{Setup.}
4	We fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-Base with LoRA rank 16, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, and 3 epochs, framing depth estimation as 5-class sequence classification (gen-0 through gen-4).\footnote{Evaluated on the original 6-generator subset; XGBoost 3-class F1\,=\,0.789. We expect 8-generator training to further improve given additional diversity; the comparison direction is preserved.}
5	For 3-class evaluation, we collapse predictions into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ post hoc.
6	All results use the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments.
7	
8	\begin{table}[h]
9	\centering
10	\small
11	\caption{QLoRA end-to-end depth classification vs.\ XGBoost on handcrafted features, under LOGO evaluation.}
12	\label{tab:qlora}
13	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
14	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
15	\toprule
16	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{5-class F1} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Per-class F1 (5-class)} \\
17	\midrule
18	XGBoost (7 features) & 0.501 $\pm$ 0.038 & 0.789 & --- \\
19	QLoRA (Qwen3-0.6B)   & 0.583 $\pm$ 0.010 & 0.905 $\pm$ 0.003 & 0.999\,/\,0.796\,/\,0.413\,/\,0.259\,/\,0.447 \\
20	\bottomrule
21	\end{tabular}}
22	\end{table}
23	
24	\paragraph{Results.}
25	QLoRA achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.003), a +11.6\,pp improvement over the XGBoost baseline (0.789).
26	On 5-class evaluation, QLoRA reaches F1\,=\,0.583 ($\pm$0.010) vs.\ 0.501 for XGBoost (+8.2\,pp), with the largest gains at gen-1 (0.796 vs.\ 0.634) and gen-2 (0.413 vs.\ 0.268).
27	The gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains the primary failure mode (gen-3 F1\,=\,0.259), consistent with the feature-level analysis in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Hyperparameter robustness.}
30	A second run with LoRA rank 32 and seed 123 yields 5-class F1\,=\,0.587 ($\pm$0.005) and 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.004), which confirms stability across hyperparameter and seed variation ($\Delta < 1$\,pp on both metrics).
31	
32	\paragraph{Implications.}
33	The substantial 3-class improvement demonstrates that raw token embeddings contain depth signal beyond what summary statistics capture; the seven handcrafted features are a strong but lossy compression of the full distributional information.
34	End-to-end fine-tuning exploits token-level patterns (e.g., positional regularities, n-gram repetitions) that aggregate features cannot represent.
35	This confirms that the depth signal documented in our main analysis is real and exploitable beyond engineered features, while the handcrafted approach retains practical advantages: interpretability, computational efficiency (no GPU inference), and the ability to reveal the differential depth response pattern that motivates the task formulation.

**结论**: WARNING

### 审计方法

逐条交叉验证 registry 全部 52 个实验条目（含 DONE + PREPARING 状态）与论文 .tex 文件中的引用。按类别分组：

- **被 v2 替代**: 2 个（plan-001 → plan-001-fix, plan-015 → plan-015-v2）→ 数据已被更新版引用
- **有结论的分析实验**: 30 个 → 逐条审查引用情况

### 发现

**[severity: warning] 1 个成功实验未被论文引用: review-exp-b-topic-drift**

实验内容：计算相邻 depth 之间的语义相似度（embedding cosine similarity），证明 depth signal ≠ topic shift。

关键数据：
- 语义相似度随 depth 递增：0→1 (0.622), 1→2 (0.683), 2→3 (0.801), 3→4 (0.859)
- 即更深的生成在语义上更接近输入，但分布特征仍能区分 depth
- Prompt-type 差异：continuation (0.717) < elaboration (0.809) ≈ rewriting (0.808)

当前论文中，appendix_seed_control.tex L27 声称 "driven by distributional properties of recursive generation, not topic identity"，但仅用 independent seed 间接论证。添加 review-exp-b-topic-drift 的语义相似度数据可以提供直接证据，使这一 claim 更难被审稿人攻击。

建议：在 appendix_seed_control.tex 末尾增加 1 段 + 可选小表，展示语义相似度随 depth 递增的数据。预计增加 4-6 行 LaTeX，不影响页数。

**[severity: info] 其余 29/30 个分析实验均已引用**

全部引用覆盖：
- 核心 LOGO 评估 (plan-002-eval)、特征消融 (plan-001-fix)、跨参考模型 (plan-003 系列)、下游 TOST (plan-004-v2)、prompt type (plan-005)、temperature 系列 (exp_047-050)、baseline 比较 (plan-015-v2)、独立种子 (exp_051)、人类编辑鲁棒性 (plan-010 系列)、文本长度控制 (plan-013)、大模型规模 (plan-014)、多域 (multi-domain-seeds + exp_047)、种子复杂度 (plan-008)、bootstrap CI (review-exp-c)
- instruct 系列 (exp_052-054) → appendix_instruct.tex Table 1
- QLoRA 系列 (exp_055/055b/056/056b) → appendix_instruct.tex Table 3 + appendix_qlora.tex

### 回答 Director 三个问题

**Q1**: 1 个未引用 — review-exp-b-topic-drift（语义相似度 vs 分布特征）

**Q2**: 可以。建议在 appendix_seed_control.tex 补充 1 段语义相似度数据，强化 "depth ≠ topic" 论点。

**Q3**: claim 强度基本已最大化。唯一可加强的点是上述 "not topic identity" 论证——当前仅有间接证据（independent seed），补上直接证据（semantic similarity 递增但 distributional features 仍区分）更稳固。

### 附：仍待处理的 2 个前轮 warning

- **W-new-1**: Abstract 用 "vocabulary tail slope"，其余全文用 "tail decay"，术语不一致
- **W-new-2**: Introduction L16 句式 "outperforming individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3pp and a 4-detector ensemble at 2.4× lower computational cost" 暗示胜过 4-detector ensemble，但实际 7-feature (0.705) < 4-det+surface (0.708)
